In a randomized study of 139 low-intermediate EFL writers assigned across four experimental conditions and a self-correction control, all four feedback groups significantly outperformed the control on grammatical errors successfully corrected during text revision (Bonilla López et al., 2018). Four weeks after feedback, learners in the direct-corrections-on-grammar, metalinguistic-codes-on-grammar, and direct-corrections-on-grammar-and-nongrammar conditions showed significantly greater long-term grammatical accuracy than the no-feedback control (Bonilla López et al., 2018). The design is a strength—random assignment, five conditions, delayed posttest—yet cognitive load was measured by self-report rather than an online physiological index (Bonilla López et al., 2018). A randomized classroom trial with 52 Iranian male learners found that a group receiving WCF outperformed controls on writing performance (Razmi & Ghane, 2024), though the small, single-sex, intermediate sample limits generalization (Razmi & Ghane, 2024).

Naturalistic work shifts attention from feedback type to learner uptake. In a naturalistic case study, AWE feedback tended to highlight rather than correct errors, and teacher feedback covered more error types (16) than AWE (8), although assignment differences may have driven this (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). The highly engaged learner outperformed the moderately engaged learner in her response to both sources of feedback and in improvements to her text (Zhang & Hyland, 2018). In an integrated approach combining automated, peer, and teacher feedback, 88% of 33 students submitted to the AWE system more than five times (M = 9.5, SD = 4.07), and most engaged behaviourally, affectively, and cognitively (Zhang & Hyland, 2021). The single-context case design limits generalizability (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).

Learner preferences add a further dimension. Survey evidence complicates this picture: students favored direct correction with metalinguistic explanation (48.10%) over correction without it (24.83%) (Liu & Wu, 2019). A synthesis of 50 classroom studies found most were qualitative (66.0%) and only 22.0% theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024).

sentences: The literature on written corrective feedback (WCF) in second-language (L2) writing is organized here around four themes: (a) the relative effects of direct and indirect feedback on accuracy, (b) revision behaviour, (c) learner engagement with teacher, peer, and automated feedback, and (d) contradictions between experimental and naturalistic findings.
Sources were drawn from applied-linguistics journals and recent syntheses; the review synthesizes by theme rather than chronology.
Experimental work reports that supplying the correct form outperforms locating errors alone.

In a randomized study of 139 low-intermediate EFL writers, all feedback groups improved immediate grammatical accuracy during revision, but a durable advantage four weeks later was evident only for direct corrections (Bonilla López et al., 2018).
The design is a strength—random assignment, five conditions, delayed posttest—yet cognitive load was measured by self-report rather than an online physiological index (Bonilla López et al., 2018).

A randomized classroom trial with 52 Iranian male learners found that a group receiving WCF outperformed controls on writing performance (Razmi & Ghane, 2024), though the small, single-sex, intermediate sample limits generalization (Razmi & Ghane, 2024).

Survey evidence complicates this picture: students favored direct correction with metalinguistic explanation (48.10%) over correction without it (24.83%) (Liu & Wu, 2019), but the non-randomized, descriptive design precludes causal claims (Liu & Wu, 2019).
Indirect feedback appears to place greater interpretive demands on writers.

In a naturalistic case study, AWE feedback tended to highlight rather than correct errors, and teacher feedback covered more error types (16) than AWE (8), although assignment differences may have driven this (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
The two-learner sample limits generalization, yet the finding that the highly engaged learner improved more on both feedback sources is suggestive (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
Engagement mediates uptake.

In an integrated approach combining automated, peer, and teacher feedback, 88% of 33 students submitted to the AWE system more than five times (M = 9.5, SD = 4.07), and most engaged behaviourally, affectively, and cognitively (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).
The single-context case design limits generalizability (Zhang & Hyland, 2021).
Findings diverge partly by design: experimental studies isolate feedback type, whereas naturalistic studies show uptake depends on learner engagement and feedback salience (Zhang & Hyland, 2018).
A synthesis of 50 classroom studies found most were qualitative (66.0%) and only 22.0% theoretically motivated (Mao et al., 2024), which helps explain inconsistent constructs across studies.

Three gaps follow: experimental evidence on long-term accuracy remains confined to a few learner populations (Bonilla López et al., 2018; Razmi & Ghane, 2024); revision and engagement research relies on small case samples (Zhang & Hyland, 2018, 2021); and most classroom studies lack theoretical framing (Mao et al., 2024).
The present study addresses these by examining direct versus indirect feedback across accuracy, revision, and engagement within a single theoretically grounded design.
These findings are taken up in the Discussion.

uncited_sentences.sentence: Direct written corrective feedback (WCF), which supplies the correct form, and indirect WCF, which locates or codes errors without supplying it, differ in the interpretive demands they place on L2 writers.
Experimental classroom evidence indicates that both forms can support accuracy gains during revision, though their durability differs.
Naturalistic work shifts attention from feedback type to learner uptake.
Learner preferences add a further dimension.
Whether these strands converge on a single account of direct versus indirect WCF remains unresolved.
